title: Linear regression and regularisation
summary: Linear regression from residuals to the normal equation, implementing it with gradient descent exactly as in the 2025 Final, multiple and polynomial regression, MSE versus MAE, and L1/L2 regularisation.
syllabus: NOAI 2025 Final Q1: linear regression by gradient descent

lessons.title: Linear regression and least squares
lessons.summary: Residuals, mean squared error, and the line that makes the total squared error smallest.
objectives: You can compute residuals and MSE for a small dataset
You can explain why squared errors are used
You can describe the loss surface over w and b

concepts.name: Residuals as squares
concepts.explain: For each point the residual is the actual value minus the prediction. Squaring residuals makes them all positive and punishes big misses heavily; the least-squares line has the smallest total squared area. The mean of these squares is the MSE.
concepts.analogy: Fitting a straight plank along stepping stones: the plank should be as close as possible to all stones, and big gaps matter most.

visual.shows: Data points with a line and an actual square drawn on each residual; the total square area and MSE are shown.
visual.interaction: Drag the line's two handles; press 'best fit' to snap to least squares; drag a single point to become an outlier and watch its square dominate.
visual.aha: Least squares literally minimises total square area, which is why outliers pull the line so strongly.

concepts.name: The loss surface over w and b
concepts.explain: Every choice of slope w and intercept b gives one MSE value, so the loss forms a surface over the (w, b) plane. For linear regression this surface is a convex bowl with a single lowest point, which is the best-fit line.
concepts.analogy: A topographic map of 'how bad' every possible plank position is, with one lowest valley.

visual.shows: A heat-map/contour of MSE over (w, b) next to the data plot; a marker on the heat-map corresponds to the line on the data.
visual.interaction: Click or drag anywhere on the heat-map to set (w, b) and see the line move; drag the line to see the marker move.
visual.aha: Fitting a line is finding the bottom of a bowl in parameter space.

checkpoint_focus: Loss surface is a convex bowl

lessons.title: Regression by gradient descent (from scratch)
lessons.summary: Deriving the MSE gradients and implementing the training loop in NumPy, exactly the 2025 Final Question 1.
objectives: You can write the gradients of MSE with respect to w and b
You can implement a vectorised gradient descent loop in NumPy
You can check convergence with the loss history

concepts.name: The gradient formula, piece by piece
concepts.explain: With predictions ŷ = Xw + b and error e = ŷ − y, the MSE gradient is ∂L/∂w = (2/n)·Xᵀe and ∂L/∂b = (2/n)·Σe. Each weight's gradient is the average of (error × its feature), so features that line up with the errors get pushed hardest.
concepts.analogy: Adjusting the volume of each speaker in a hall by how much it contributed to the noise complaint.

visual.shows: A table of 5 data points with columns x, y, ŷ, e and e·x filling step by step, then summed and scaled into the gradient, then the parameter update.
visual.interaction: Step through the computation; edit w and b to see the gradient change sign.
visual.aha: The gradient is a weighted average of errors, which you can compute by hand for a small table.

concepts.name: Watching the line learn
concepts.explain: Each iteration computes predictions, the error, the gradients and an update. Plotting the loss after each iteration should show a steady decrease; a rising or exploding loss means the learning rate is too high.
concepts.analogy: Practising free throws: each attempt you adjust slightly based on how you missed, and your miss distance shrinks over time.

visual.shows: Three linked panels: the data with the current line, the (w, b) contour map with the path so far, and the loss-versus-iteration curve.
visual.interaction: Play or step; set the learning rate and iterations; restart from a different initial line.
visual.aha: The line on the data, the dot in parameter space and the falling loss curve are three views of one process.

concepts.name: Simultaneous updates and the ½ convention
concepts.explain: Many textbooks and the 2025 Final write the loss as (1/2m)·Σ(ŷ − y)², so the 2 from differentiating cancels and the gradient is (1/m)·Xᵀ(Xθ − y). That only rescales the learning rate, but with a fixed number of iterations it changes the rounded answer: on the 2025 data, 1000 steps at α = 0.01 give θ ≈ [0.003, 0.9987] with 1/m but [0.0, 1.0] with 2/m. If X already contains an intercept column, θ includes the bias, so do not add a separate b. Update all parameters from the same predictions: changing θ₀ first and then using it to update θ₁ is a different algorithm (it gives [0.0027, 0.9988] here). The line theta -= alpha * X.T @ (X @ theta - y) / m does it correctly.
concepts.analogy: A group photo where everyone adjusts their position based on the same snapshot, rather than each person moving after watching the previous person move.

visual.shows: The 2025 Final data (X = [[2, 2], [2, 4], [2, 6]], y = [2, 4, 6]) with θ after each iteration for three versions side by side: vectorised, a loop with a temporary copy, and a buggy sequential loop, compared with the expected [0.003, 0.9987].
visual.interaction: Run or step the iterations; toggle the ½ convention to see the effective learning rate and the 4-decimal answer change; switch the intercept column on and off.
visual.aha: Simultaneous updates and the same constants as the specification are what make your answer match the official one to four decimal places.

checkpoint_focus: Effect of learning rate and iterations
Simultaneous update; 1/m versus 2/m; intercept column already in X

lessons.title: Multiple and polynomial regression
lessons.summary: Many features in matrix form, the normal equation, and curves from polynomial features.
objectives: You can write predictions for many features as Xw
You can state the normal equation w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy and when it fails
You can fit curves with polynomial features

concepts.name: Matrix form and the normal equation
concepts.explain: With n examples and d features, X has shape (n, d) and the predictions are Xw. Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equation w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, a one-shot solution. It fails if XᵀX is singular (for example duplicated features), where the pseudoinverse still gives an answer; for huge d, gradient descent is cheaper.
concepts.analogy: Solving for the answer with a formula versus walking downhill step by step to the same place.

visual.shows: The shapes of X, Xᵀ, XᵀX, Xᵀy and w as labelled blocks multiplying together, and the resulting weights compared with gradient descent's answer.
visual.interaction: Change n and d with sliders; add a duplicated feature column and see XᵀX become singular.
visual.aha: The closed form is a few matrix products whose shapes you can check, but it needs XᵀX to be invertible.

concepts.name: Curves from straight-line maths
concepts.explain: Adding features x², x³ lets a linear model fit curves, because the model is still linear in its weights: y = w₀ + w₁x + w₂x² + w₃x³. Higher degrees fit more wiggles and risk overfitting.
concepts.analogy: Lego bricks are straight, but enough of them can build a curved arch.

visual.shows: Basis curves 1, x, x², x³ scaled by weight sliders and their sum overlaid on data points.
visual.interaction: Slide each weight; press 'fit' to set them by least squares; increase the degree.
visual.aha: 'Linear' regression means linear in the weights, not a straight line.

checkpoint_focus: Polynomial features are still linear in w

lessons.title: L1 and L2 regularisation
lessons.summary: Penalising large weights to reduce overfitting; why L2 shrinks weights smoothly and L1 sets some exactly to zero; MSE versus MAE.
objectives: You can write the ridge (L2) and lasso (L1) losses
You can explain why L1 produces sparse weights
You can predict the effect of increasing λ (and of scikit-learn's C)
You can compare MSE and MAE on outliers

concepts.name: Penalty shapes: circle versus diamond
concepts.explain: Regularisation adds a penalty on weight size to the loss. Picture the allowed weights as a region: L2 (ridge) uses a circle, L1 (lasso) a diamond. The best fit is where the loss contours first touch the region, and for the diamond that is often a corner, where one weight is exactly zero.
concepts.analogy: Packing a suitcase under an airline weight limit: L1 makes you leave whole items behind, L2 makes you pack lighter versions of everything.

visual.shows: Elliptical loss contours around the unregularised optimum and the L1 diamond or L2 circle; the constrained solution is marked where they touch, with its coordinates.
visual.interaction: Drag the unregularised optimum; slide the constraint size; toggle L1 and L2.
visual.aha: L1's corners make exact zeros likely, so it performs feature selection; L2 just shrinks.

concepts.name: Regularisation paths
concepts.explain: As the penalty strength λ grows, all weights shrink; under lasso they hit zero one after another. Too much regularisation underfits. In scikit-learn's LogisticRegression and SVC, C = 1/λ, so a smaller C means stronger regularisation. The intercept is usually not penalised.
concepts.analogy: Turning down the bass, mid and treble together; with lasso some knobs click fully off.

visual.shows: Coefficient bars for 6 features and a plot of each coefficient against log λ, with validation error underneath.
visual.interaction: Slide λ (or C); toggle ridge or lasso; find the λ with the lowest validation error.
visual.aha: There is a sweet spot of regularisation, and C moves in the opposite direction to λ.

concepts.name: MSE versus MAE
concepts.explain: MSE squares errors, so one big error dominates; MAE takes absolute values, so it is more robust to outliers. The MSE-optimal constant prediction is the mean; the MAE-optimal constant is the median. Huber loss behaves like MSE for small errors and MAE for big ones.
concepts.analogy: MSE is a strict teacher who punishes one disastrous answer heavily; MAE treats every mark lost equally.

visual.shows: A dataset with two lines fitted by MSE and MAE, plus each loss as a function of a single residual.
visual.interaction: Drag one point far away as an outlier and watch the MSE line swing while the MAE line barely moves.
visual.aha: Your loss function encodes how much you fear big mistakes.
